    "description": "As part of this interview, Satya Nadella gave me and Dylan Patel (founder of SemiAnalysis) an exclusive first-look at their brand-new Fairwater 2 datacenter.\n\nMicrosoft is building multiple Fairwaters, each of which has hundreds of thousands of GB200s & GB300s. Between all these interconnected buildings, they’ll have over 2 GW of total capacity. Just to give a frame of reference, even a single one of these Fairwater buildings is more powerful than any other AI datacenter that currently exists.\n\nSatya then answered a bunch of questions about how Microsoft is preparing for AGI across all layers of the stack.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/satya-nadella-2\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/satya-nadella-how-microsoft-is-preparing-for-agi/id1516093381?i=1000736461892\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/290a568fldDQBrPhYOCZFK?si=71a120f868384ffd\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n* Labelbox produces high-quality data at massive scale, powering any capability you want your model to have.       "id": "Ugy9ORw6WgL_3WNTM1Z4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The T-44 is one of the lesser-known but highly influential Soviet medium tanks of the mid-20th century. Developed during the final years of the Second World War, it served as the crucial bridge between the legendary T-34 and the globally recognized T-54/55 series. Although it saw limited combat and production numbers were modest, the T-44 introduced several groundbreaking design features that shaped tank development for decades.\n\nThe T-44 tank represents a pivotal but often overlooked transition in Soviet armored development. It successfully addressed many shortcomings of the T-34 while laying the structural and conceptual foundations for the iconic tanks that defined the Cold War.\n\nThough it never achieved the fame of its predecessors or successors, the T-44’s innovative engineering made it one of the most important steps in the evolution of modern tank design.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCtlOnR4vywADS_c919fiTaA",

      "parent": "Ugxram1MfgtLnJKwPvZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Or you could think of it this way: coders are the early adopters of AI just as IT people and academics were the early adopters of the internet. Then, as the technology got better, it's usefulness widened. As the usefulness widened and adoption expanded, there was more money to put into advancing the technology. This virtuous cycle resulted in a revolution.\n\nI grew up during that time and I can remember the world before the internet. Some futurists at the time who predicted amazing things sounded like fiction writers.       "text": "The cloud businesss is elastic and prone to fulfill demand with capacity over provisioning.     {
      "id": "Ugw-TCWX94ydRilU3Dd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I abhor these questions. They forced him into a defensive equilibrium.\n\nHis actual value is his systems-level mental model of scaling intelligence infrastructure. When the questions shift to “justify your partnership” or “explain your moat,” he drops into corporate-safe mode. That collapses the signal.\n\nThey could have extracted his real framework:\n\n1. Constraint hierarchy\nHow he ranks power, cooling, interconnect, scheduling, and software-efficiency as limiting factors. That reveals his internal physics model of compute.\n\n2. Temporal cadence of breakthroughs\nHow he expects architectural, silicon, and algorithmic improvements to stack. That shows his mental map of AI as an evolving dynamical system, not a revenue stream.\n\n3. Phase transitions in capability\nHis view on when systems shift from tool-like to agentic. That exposes his criteria for structural breaks rather than marketing narratives.\n\n4. Interaction between global regulation and model design\nHe has a detailed picture of how geopolitics shapes model heterogeneity. That’s strategy, not market-share defense.\n\n5. Co-design logic\nHis internal calculus for when to build hardware vs buy. That is a pure engineering optimization problem.\n\n6. Organizational physics\nHe thinks deeply about why large enterprises adopt slowly even when tech is nonlinear. You get insight into second-order effects and friction in socio-technical systems.\n\nThose are the questions that reveal how Nadella reasons under uncertainty. Instead they asked questions that forced him to restate approved positions.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "They are screwed when it turns out the chips they have and the architecture they have are not the ones needed for AGI. You can't just pivot away from that massive investment. None of the hyperscalers today that are going all in and pouring all this capex today are gonna survive and be the ones to get AGI.\n\nIt'll be some small AI company that is agile and nimble who'll take all the advancements done by the hyperscalers and use it to build the first AGI.\n\nThe most that they can get out of the data centers they are building today are useful agents. Good at specific tasks but bad at generalizing.\n\nThey will get destroyed when AGI comes around. There's no \"catching up\" to the first company to build it.       "id": "UgyhHu9EEJQpixMWGFZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Given everything you shared (and assuming you care about AI strategy more than touristic data-center shots), I’d pick these:\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n### If you want ONE continuous ~15-minute chunk\r\n\r\n*Watch: 20:56 – 36:00*\r\n\r\nThis gives you, in one arc:\r\n\r\n1. *“Whose margins will expand most?” (20:56–~29:30)*\r\n\r\n   * Models vs “scaffolding” (Office, GitHub, infra).\r\n   * Nadella’s argument that models may commoditize, while value accrues to whoever owns data, grounding, and orchestration.\r\n   * Deep dive into Excel Agent and what it means to embed a model into mid-tier logic rather than just wrapping an API.\r\n   * His vision of fully autonomous AI “employees” and how Microsoft pivots from per-user SaaS to per-agent infra.\r\n\r\n2. *Transition to infra + hybrid agent/human world (29:30–~36:00)*\r\n\r\n   * Two futures: tools for humans vs infra for autonomous agents.\r\n   * Why even in an agent-only world you still need identity, observability, storage, compliance.\r\n   * How AI-driven migration (Excel → DBs, mainframe → cloud, etc.) reshapes Microsoft’s stack.\r\n\r\nIf you only watch one segment, this is the densest mix of economics, product, and long-term architecture.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n### If you’re okay with JUMPING between excerpts (~15 minutes total)\r\n\r\n#### 1) 04:15 – 11:15 (~7 minutes) – *Business models for AGI + macro view*\r\n\r\nWhy: Sets up his philosophical and economic frame.\r\n\r\nKey bits:\r\n\r\n* AGI as “guardian angel” + “cognitive amplifier”.\r\n* Diffusion vs hype: why true productivity shows up only when workflows change.\r\n* How they think about subscriptions as “entitlements to consumption” (compute/tokens).\r\n* Lessons from cloud migration → analogy for AI monetization and margin structure.\r\n\r\n#### 2) 20:56 – 28:30 (~7–8 minutes) – *Models vs scaffolding + Excel Agent*\r\n\r\nWhy: This is the sharpest section if you care about value capture and product design.\r\n\r\nKey bits:\r\n\r\n* Will models capture all the margin, or will scaffolding + data win?\r\n* The “winner’s curse” for model labs if their checkpoints are easily replicated.\r\n* Excel Agent as an example of embedding a cognitive layer into an existing system.\r\n* Early picture of the “per-agent” business model and infra stack.\r\n\r\nThese two excerpts together give you ~14–15 minutes and cover:\r\n\r\n* How Nadella thinks about AGI economically.\r\n* Where profit pools might form (models vs infra vs apps).\r\n* How that translates into concrete product decisions (Excel Agent, Copilot, agents-as-workers).\r\n\r\nIf you want to add a tiny “bonus” 3–4 minutes after that, I’d tack on *37:12 – 40:30* just to hear his take on MAI vs OpenAI and how he plans to avoid wasting flops duplicating GPT.",

      "text": "I think the biggest takeaway is that Satya doesn't really believe in AGI within a decade, he believes in powerful but still narrow AI tools, and this will basically be a normal technology with multiple competing AI companies, each with their own own comparative advantage.     {
      "id": "Ugytkxa9VlzT0r-BVQZ4AaABAg.APSd0AMyNdaAPi2foUtkYV",
      "parent": "Ugytkxa9VlzT0r-BVQZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "AGI is the dream of every researcher, but it won’t come easily.\nAI development has moved from the algorithmic competitions of the Hinton–LeCun–Bengio or Andrew Ng era, through a battle over the amount of data, and now into a race defined by semiconductor compute speed.\n\nIn a way, it resembles how humans prepare for exams:\nyou need a good brain, you need to fill it with a lot of information, and ultimately you need the stamina to study for a long time.\n\nSeeing that even modern LLMs now rely more on MECHANICS than on TECHNIQUES, AGI — which must integrate and reason across vast domains of information — may require an entirely new level of underlying mechanics before it can truly emerge.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCXE_JW23gYDKDst1HbiF50w",
      "author": "@whatever_debate",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/TKvc3vC-hm5TYFrSWUtQ_rKo4xGs9TF5opSjTpLXn93g2llY0gHL9mCGJOPh_pvT9xWDZyKmAw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxmkECDKkwdm7Bp1Vd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "\"Satya Nadella – How Microsoft is preparing for AGI\":\r\n\r\nExclusive Tour & Datacenter Power: The interview begins with Satya Nadella and Scott Guthrie (EVP, Cloud and AI) showcasing Microsoft’s new Fairwater 2 datacenter—currently the world’s most powerful AI datacenter. Microsoft is scaling infrastructure aggressively, aiming to 10x training capacity every 18–24 months. The facilities are built to support enormous workloads, including future large-scale models that may need resources spanning multiple datacenters.\r\n\r\nAI & Business Models: Nadella discusses the fast acceleration of technological revolutions and how AI/AGI is the biggest yet. He emphasizes we're in the early innings, with scaling laws working but many breakthroughs still needed. AI should serve as a “cognitive amplifier” and “guardian angel”—a tool that enhances human utility, but also represents a significant business opportunity.\r\n\r\nMonetization, SaaS, & Market Expansion: The move from selling boxed software to cloud subscriptions (e.g., Office 365) massively expanded Microsoft’s market. Nadella notes that while AI SaaS has high costs (COGS), it also greatly increases accessibility and utility. Microsoft anticipates further expansion, with millions of new GitHub repos and users driven by AI coding assistants like Copilot.\r\n\r\nCompetitive Landscape: The AI/coding assistant market is becoming crowded, but Microsoft believes that competition and market growth are both healthy. While Microsoft’s dominance (e.g., with VS Code and GitHub) is challenged, the total addressable market is rapidly expanding.\r\n\r\nInnovation & Model Strategy: Microsoft is pursuing a multi-layered approach:\r\n\r\nInfrastructure: Build flexible, fungible environments—not over-optimizing for any one model or use-case.\r\n\r\nModel Layer: Access to OpenAI models, internal MAI (Microsoft AI) models, frontier partnerships (e.g., with Anthropic), and ongoing internal development.\r\n\r\n“Scaffolding” Layer: Integrate and extend models deeply into products, such as Office 365’s “Excel Agent”, not just as UI wrappers but embedding native product logic into AI behavior.\r\n\r\nFlexible Model & Open Competition: Nadella stresses that there will not be a single “winner-take-all” AGI model; multiple models and open source solutions will coexist, serving different geographies, sectors, and applications.\r\n\r\nTransition to Agentic World: The future involves not just human users but autonomous agents leveraging Microsoft’s platforms. Companies may provision computers and tools for both users and autonomous AI agents, with Microsoft aiming to support both scenarios through its infrastructure and tooling.\r\n\r\nDatacenter Investment & Global Strategy: Microsoft continues to scale its hyperscaler fleet, adjusting construction strategies for flexibility, energy, and regional requirements. Nadella is wary of over-investing in one generation of hardware and keeps a global, long-term perspective.\r\n\r\nSovereignty, Policy, and Trust: As governments worry about AI sovereignty and data locality, Microsoft is building “sovereign clouds” (e.g., in Europe and India) and working closely with policy requirements. Nadella believes global trust in American technology and US-based companies is essential, but acknowledges bipolar (US-China) and regional AI strategies will shape the competitive landscape.\r\n\r\nR&D, Talent, and Future-Proofing: Massive capital is being invested not only in hardware but also in acquiring AI research talent. Microsoft is assembling world-class teams alongside keeping access to OpenAI’s advancements. Nadella sees a future where models may learn continuously, amplifying the value of whoever is ahead.\r\n\r\nOverall:\r\nMicrosoft’s AGI/AI vision is not just about chasing the biggest model. It’s about building a flexible, global infrastructure; deeply integrating AI into every layer of their software ecosystem; fostering a healthy competitive landscape with both proprietary and open-source models; and earning institutional trust with sovereign-respecting approaches. Nadella presents Microsoft as a software, infrastructure, and knowledge company—fully preparing to support both human and agent-driven work in the coming AGI era.​",

## Description

As part of this interview, Satya Nadella gave me and Dylan Patel (founder of SemiAnalysis) an exclusive first-look at their brand-new Fairwater 2 datacenter.

Microsoft is building multiple Fairwaters, each of which has hundreds of thousands of GB200s & GB300s. Between all these interconnected buildings, they’ll have over 2 GW of total capacity. Just to give a frame of reference, even a single one of these Fairwater buildings is more powerful than any other AI datacenter that currently exists.

Satya then answered a bunch of questions about how Microsoft is preparing for AGI across all layers of the stack.

integration needed, knowing that as long as&nbsp;&nbsp; you're serving the market well with the&nbsp; product, you can always cost-optimize.&nbsp; There's a question going forward.&nbsp; Right now, we have models that have&nbsp;&nbsp;

any one model, that is not the case.&nbsp; Take coding, there are multiple models. In fact, everyday it's less the case.&nbsp; There is not one model that&nbsp; is getting deployed broadly.&nbsp;

There are multiple models that are getting&nbsp; deployed. It's like databases. It's always&nbsp;&nbsp; the thing, "Can one database be the one that&nbsp; is just used everywhere?" Except it's not.&nbsp;&nbsp; There are multiple types of databases that&nbsp;

are getting deployed for different use cases.&nbsp; I think that there are going to be some&nbsp; network effects of continual learning—I&nbsp;&nbsp; call it data liquidity—that any one model has. Is it going to happen in all domains? I don't&nbsp;&nbsp;

think so. Is it going to happen in all geos?&nbsp; I don't think so. Is it going to happen in all&nbsp;&nbsp; segments? I don't think so. It'll happen in all&nbsp; categories at the same time? I don't think so.&nbsp;&nbsp; So therefore I feel like the design space is&nbsp;

so large that there's plenty of opportunity.&nbsp; But your fundamental point is having a capability&nbsp; which is at the infrastructure layer, model layer,&nbsp;&nbsp; and at the scaffolding layer, and then&nbsp; being able to compose these things not&nbsp;&nbsp;

just as a vertical stack, but to be able to&nbsp; compose each thing for what its purpose is.&nbsp; You can't build an infrastructure&nbsp; that's optimized for one model.&nbsp; If you do that, what if you fall behind?

In fact, all the infrastructure&nbsp;&nbsp; you built will be a waste. You kind of need to build an&nbsp;&nbsp; infrastructure that's capable of supporting&nbsp; multiple families and lineages of models.&nbsp;

Otherwise the capital you put in, which is&nbsp; optimized for one model architecture, means&nbsp;&nbsp; you're one tweak away, some MoE-like breakthrough&nbsp; that happens, and your entire network topology&nbsp;&nbsp; goes out of the window. That's a scary thing.&nbsp;

Therefore you kind of want the infrastructure&nbsp;&nbsp; to support whatever may come in your own model&nbsp; family and other model families. You've got to&nbsp;&nbsp; be open. If you're serious about the hyperscale&nbsp; business, you've got to be serious about that.&nbsp;

If you're serious about being a model&nbsp; company, you have to basically say,&nbsp;&nbsp; "What are the ways people can do things on top of&nbsp; the model so that I can have an ISV ecosystem?"&nbsp; Unless I'm thinking I'll own every&nbsp;

category, that just can't be that.&nbsp; Then you won't have an API business and that, by&nbsp; definition, will mean you'll never be a platform&nbsp;&nbsp; company that's successfully deployed everywhere. Therefore the industry structure is such that&nbsp;&nbsp;

it will really force people to specialize. In that specialization, a company like Microsoft&nbsp;&nbsp; should compete in each layer by its merits, but&nbsp; not think that this is all about the road to game&nbsp;&nbsp; set match, where I just compose vertically&nbsp;

all these layers. That just doesn't happen.&nbsp; So last year Microsoft was on path to be&nbsp; the largest infrastructure provider by far.&nbsp; You were the earliest in 2023, so you went&nbsp; out there, you acquired all the resources&nbsp;&nbsp;

in terms of leasing data centers, starting&nbsp; construction, securing power, everything.&nbsp; You guys were on pace to&nbsp; beat Amazon in 2026 or 2027.&nbsp; Certainly by 2028 you were going to beat them.

Since then, let’s call it, in the second half&nbsp;&nbsp; of last year, Microsoft did this big pause, where&nbsp; they let go of a bunch of leasing sites that they&nbsp;&nbsp; were going to take, which then Google, Meta,&nbsp; Amazon in some cases, Oracle, took these sites.&nbsp;

We're sitting in one of the largest data centers&nbsp; in the world, so obviously it's not everything,&nbsp;&nbsp; you guys are expanding like crazy. But there are sites that you just stopped&nbsp;&nbsp; working on. Why did you do this?

This goes back a little bit to,&nbsp;&nbsp; what is the hyperscale business all about? One of the key decisions we made was that&nbsp;&nbsp; if we're going to build out Azure to&nbsp; be fantastic for all stages of AI—from&nbsp;&nbsp;

training to mid-training to data gen to&nbsp; inference—we just need fungibility of the fleet.&nbsp; So that entire thing caused us basically&nbsp; not to go build a whole lot of capacity&nbsp;&nbsp; with a particular set of generations.

Because the other thing you have to&nbsp;&nbsp; realize is that having up to now 10x'ed&nbsp; every 18 months enough training capacity&nbsp;&nbsp; for the various OpenAI models, we realized&nbsp; that the key is to stay on that path.&nbsp;

But the more important thing is to have a balance,&nbsp; to not just train, but to be able to serve these&nbsp;&nbsp; models all around the world. Because at the end of the day,&nbsp;&nbsp; the rate of monetization is what&nbsp;

will then allow us to keep funding.&nbsp; And then the infrastructure was going&nbsp; to need us to support multiple models.&nbsp; So once we said that that's the case, we&nbsp; just course-corrected to the path we're on.&nbsp;

If I look at the path we're on, we&nbsp; are doing a lot more starts now.&nbsp; We are also buying up as much managed&nbsp; capacity as we can, whether it's to build,&nbsp;&nbsp; whether it's to lease, or even GPUs as a service.

But we're building it for where we see the demand&nbsp;&nbsp; and the serving needs and our training needs. We didn't want to just be a hoster for one company&nbsp;&nbsp; and have just a massive book&nbsp; of business with one customer.&nbsp;

That's not a business, you should be&nbsp; vertically integrated with that company.&nbsp; Given that OpenAI was going to be&nbsp; a successful independent company,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is fantastic. It makes sense. And even&nbsp;

Meta may use third-party capacity, but ultimately&nbsp;&nbsp; they're all going to be first-party. For anyone who has large scale,&nbsp;&nbsp; they'll be a hyperscaler on their own. To me, it was to build out a hyperscale&nbsp;&nbsp;

fleet and our own research compute. That's what&nbsp; the adjustment was. So I feel very, very good.&nbsp; By the way, the other thing is that I didn't want&nbsp; to get stuck with massive scale of one generation.&nbsp; We just saw the GB200s, the GB300s are coming.

By the time I get to Vera Rubin, Vera Rubin Ultra,&nbsp;&nbsp; the data center is going to look very different&nbsp; because the power per rack, power per row,&nbsp;&nbsp; is going to be so different. The cooling requirements are&nbsp;&nbsp;

going to be so different. That means I don't want to&nbsp;&nbsp; just go build out a whole number of gigawatts&nbsp; that are only for a one-generation, one family.&nbsp; So I think the pacing matters, the&nbsp;

fungibility and the location matters,&nbsp;&nbsp; the workload diversity matters, customer diversity&nbsp; matters and that's what we’re building towards.&nbsp; The other thing that we've learned&nbsp; a lot is that every AI workload does&nbsp;&nbsp;

require not only the AI accelerator, but&nbsp; it requires a whole lot of other things.&nbsp; In fact, a lot of the margin structure&nbsp; for us will be in those other things.&nbsp; Therefore, we want to build out Azure as being&nbsp;

fantastic for the long tail of the workloads,&nbsp;&nbsp; because that's the hyperscale business, while&nbsp; knowing that we've got to be super competitive&nbsp;&nbsp; starting with the bare-metal&nbsp; for the highest end training.&nbsp;

But that can't crowd out the rest of the&nbsp; business, because we're not in the business&nbsp;&nbsp; of just doing five contracts with five customers&nbsp; being their bare-metal service. That's not a&nbsp;&nbsp; Microsoft business. That may be a business&nbsp;

for someone else, and that's a good thing.&nbsp; What we have said is that we're in the&nbsp; hyperscale business, which is at the end&nbsp;&nbsp; of the day a long tail business for AI workloads. And in order to do that, we will have some leading&nbsp;&nbsp;

bare-metal-as-a-service capabilities&nbsp; for a set of models, including our own.&nbsp; And that, I think, is the balance you see. Another question that comes around&nbsp;&nbsp; this whole fungibility topic.

Okay, it's not where you want it, you would&nbsp;&nbsp; rather have it in a good population center, like&nbsp; Atlanta. We're here. There's also the question of,&nbsp;&nbsp; how much does that matter as the horizon of AI&nbsp; tasks grows? 30 seconds for a reasoning prompt,&nbsp;&nbsp;

or 30 minutes for a deep research, or it's going&nbsp; to be hours for software agents at some point&nbsp;&nbsp; and days and so on and so forth,&nbsp; the time to human interaction.&nbsp; Why does it matter if it's location A, B, or C?

It’s a great question. That's exactly it. In fact,&nbsp;&nbsp; that's one of the other reasons why we want to&nbsp; think about what an Azure region looks like and&nbsp;&nbsp; what is the networking between Azure regions. This is where I think as the model capabilities&nbsp;&nbsp;

evolve and the usage of these tokens evolves,&nbsp; whether it's synchronously or asynchronously,&nbsp;&nbsp; you don't want to be out of position. Then on top of that, by the way,&nbsp;&nbsp; what are the data residency laws?

There’s the entire EU thing, where&nbsp;&nbsp; we literally had to create an EU Data Boundary. That basically meant that you can't just roundtrip&nbsp;&nbsp; a call to wherever, even if it's asynchronous. Therefore you need to have maybe regional&nbsp;&nbsp;

things that are high density, and&nbsp; then the power costs and so on.&nbsp; But you're 100% right in bringing up that the&nbsp; topology as we build out will have to evolve.&nbsp; One, for tokens per dollar per watt. What&nbsp;

are the economics? Overlay that with,&nbsp;&nbsp; what is the usage pattern? Usage pattern in terms&nbsp;&nbsp; of synchronous, asynchronous. But also what is the compute storage?&nbsp;

Because the latencies may matter for certain&nbsp; things. The storage better be there. If I have&nbsp;&nbsp; a Cosmos DB close to this for session data or even&nbsp; for an autonomous thing, then that also has to be&nbsp;&nbsp; somewhere close to it, and so on.

All of those considerations are&nbsp;&nbsp; what will shape the hyperscale business. Prior to the pause, what we had forecasted for&nbsp;&nbsp; you, by 2028 you were going to be 12–13 gigawatts. Now we're at nine and a half or so.&nbsp;

But something that's even more relevant—and&nbsp; I just want you to more concretely state that&nbsp;&nbsp; this is the business you don't want to be&nbsp; in—is that Oracle's going from 1/5th your&nbsp;&nbsp; size to bigger than you by the end of 2027.

While it's not a Microsoft-level quality of&nbsp;&nbsp; return on invested capital, they're&nbsp; still making 35% gross margins.&nbsp; So the question is, maybe it's not Microsoft's&nbsp; business to do this, but you've created a&nbsp;&nbsp;

hyperscaler now by refusing this business, by&nbsp; giving away the right of first refusal, et cetera.&nbsp; First of all, I don't want to take away&nbsp; anything from the success Oracle has had in&nbsp;&nbsp; building their business and I wish them well.

The thing that I think I've answered for you&nbsp;&nbsp; is that it didn't make sense for us to&nbsp; go be a hoster for one model company&nbsp;&nbsp; with limited time horizon RPO. Let's just put it that way.&nbsp;

The thing that you have to think through&nbsp; is not what you do in the next five years,&nbsp;&nbsp; but what you do for the next 50. We made our set of decisions.&nbsp; I feel very good about our OpenAI&nbsp;

partnership and what we're doing.&nbsp; We have a decent book of business. We wish them a lot of success.&nbsp; In fact, we are buyers of Oracle capacity.&nbsp; We wish them success. But at this point,&nbsp;&nbsp;

I think the industrial logic for what we are&nbsp; trying to do is pretty clear, which is that it's&nbsp;&nbsp; not about chasing… First of all, I track, by&nbsp; the way, your things whether it's AWS or Google&nbsp;&nbsp; and ours, which I think is super useful.

But it doesn't mean I have to chase those.&nbsp; I have to chase them for not just the gross margin&nbsp; that they may represent in a period of time.&nbsp; What is this book of business that&nbsp; Microsoft uniquely can go clear, which&nbsp;&nbsp;

makes sense for us to clear? That's what we'll do. I have a question even stepping back from this,&nbsp;&nbsp; I take your point that it's a better business&nbsp; to be in, all else equal, to have a long tail&nbsp;&nbsp; of customers you can have higher margin from&nbsp;

rather than serving bare metal to a few labs.&nbsp; But then there's a question of,&nbsp; which way is the industry evolving?&nbsp; If we believe we're on the path to smarter&nbsp; and smarter AIs, then why isn't the shape of&nbsp;&nbsp;

the industry that the OpenAIs and Anthropics and&nbsp; DeepMinds are the platform on which the long tail&nbsp;&nbsp; of enterprises are actually doing business? They need bare metal, but they are the platform.&nbsp; What is the long tail that&nbsp;

is directly using Azure?&nbsp; Because you want to use&nbsp; the general cognitive core.&nbsp; But those models are all going to be available&nbsp; on Azure, so any workload that says, "Hey,&nbsp;&nbsp;

I want to use some open source model and an&nbsp; OpenAI model," if you go to Azure Foundry today,&nbsp;&nbsp; you have all these models that you can&nbsp; provision, buy PTUs, get a Cosmos DB,&nbsp;&nbsp; get a SQL DB, get some storage, get some compute.

That's what a real workload looks like.&nbsp; A real workload is not just&nbsp; an API call to a model.&nbsp; A real workload needs all of these things to&nbsp; go build an app or instantiate an application.&nbsp;

In fact, the model companies&nbsp; need that to build anything.&nbsp; It's not just like, "I have a token factory." I have to have all of these things. That's&nbsp;&nbsp; the hyperscale business. And it's not on&nbsp;

any one model, but all of these models.&nbsp; So if you want Grok plus, say, OpenAI plus&nbsp; an open source model, come to Azure Foundry,&nbsp;&nbsp; provision them, build your application. Here is&nbsp; a database. That's kind of what the business is.&nbsp;

There is a separate business called just selling&nbsp; raw bare-metal services to model companies.&nbsp; And that's the argument about&nbsp; how much of that business you&nbsp;&nbsp; want to be in and not be in and what that is.

It's a very different segment of the business,&nbsp;&nbsp; which we are in, and we also have limits to how&nbsp; much of it is going to crowd out the rest of it.&nbsp; But that's kind of at least the way I look at it.&nbsp; There are sort of two questions here.

One is, why couldn't you just do both?&nbsp; The other one is, given our estimates&nbsp; on what your capacity is in 2028,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's three and a half gigawatts lower. Sure, you could have dedicated that to&nbsp;&nbsp;

OpenAI training and inference capacity,&nbsp; but you could have also dedicated that&nbsp;&nbsp; to actually just running Azure, running&nbsp; Microsoft 365, running GitHub Copilot.&nbsp; I could have just built it&nbsp;

and not given it to OpenAI.&nbsp; Or I may want to build it in a different location. I may want to build it in the UAE,&nbsp;&nbsp; I may want to build it in India,&nbsp; I may want to build it in Europe.&nbsp;

One of the things is, as I said, where we have&nbsp; real capacity constraints right now, given&nbsp;&nbsp; the regulatory needs and the data sovereignty&nbsp; needs, we've got to build all over the world.&nbsp; First of all, stateside capacity is super&nbsp;

important, and we want to build everything.&nbsp; But when I look out to 2030, I have a&nbsp; global view of what is Microsoft's shape&nbsp;&nbsp; of business by first-party and third-party. Third-party segmented by the frontier labs&nbsp;&nbsp;

and how much they want versus the inference&nbsp; capacity we want to build for multiple models,&nbsp;&nbsp; and our own research compute needs. That's all going into my calculus.&nbsp; You're rightfully pointing out the pause,&nbsp;

but the pause was not done because we said,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Oh my God, we don't want to build that." We realized that we want to build what we want&nbsp;&nbsp; to build slightly differently by both workload&nbsp; type as well as geo-type and timing as well.&nbsp;

We'll keep ramping up our gigawatts, and the&nbsp; question is at what pace and in what location.&nbsp; And how do I ride Moore's law on it, which is,&nbsp; do I really want to overbuild three and a half&nbsp;&nbsp; in 2027 or do I want to spread that in 2027-28&nbsp;

knowing even… One of the biggest learnings we had&nbsp;&nbsp; even with Nvidia is that their pace increased&nbsp; in terms of their migrations. That was a big&nbsp;&nbsp; factor. I didn't want to go get stuck for four&nbsp; or five years of depreciation on one generation.&nbsp;

In fact, Jensen's advice to me was two things. One is, get on the speed-of-light execution.&nbsp; That's why the execution in&nbsp; this Atlanta data center....&nbsp; I mean, it's like 90 days between when we&nbsp;

get it and to hand off to a real workload.&nbsp; That's real speed-of-light&nbsp; execution on that front.&nbsp; I wanted to get good on that. And then that way I'm building&nbsp;&nbsp;

each generation in scaling. And then every five years,&nbsp;&nbsp; you have something much more balanced. So it becomes literally like a flow&nbsp;&nbsp; for a large-scale industrial operation like&nbsp;

this where you're suddenly not lopsided,&nbsp;&nbsp; where you've built up a lot in one time and then&nbsp; you take a massive hiatus because you're stuck&nbsp;&nbsp; with all this, to your point, in one location&nbsp; which may be great for training, or it may not&nbsp;&nbsp;

be great for inference because I can't serve,&nbsp; even if it's all asynchronous, because Europe&nbsp;&nbsp; won't let me round-trip to Texas. So that's all of the things.&nbsp; How do I rationalize this statement with&nbsp;

what you've done over the last few weeks?&nbsp; You've announced deals with Iris&nbsp; Energy, with Nebius, and Lambda Labs,&nbsp;&nbsp; and there's a few more coming as well. You're going out there and securing capacity&nbsp;&nbsp;

that you're renting from the neoclouds&nbsp; rather than having built it yourself.&nbsp; It's fine for us because now when you have line&nbsp; of sight to demand, which can be served where&nbsp;&nbsp; people are building, it's great.

In fact we will take leases,&nbsp;&nbsp; we will take build-to-suit, we'll even take&nbsp; GPUs-as-a-service where we don't have capacity&nbsp;&nbsp; but we need capacity and someone else has that. And by the way, I would even sort of welcome every&nbsp;&nbsp;

neocloud to just be part of our marketplace.&nbsp; Because guess what? If they go bring their&nbsp;&nbsp; capacity into our marketplace, that customer who&nbsp; comes through Azure will use the neocloud, which&nbsp;&nbsp; is a great win for them, and will use compute,&nbsp;

storage, databases, all the rest from Azure.&nbsp; So I'm not at all thinking of this as, "Hey, I&nbsp; should just go gobble up all of that myself."&nbsp; You mentioned how this depreciating asset, in five&nbsp; or six years, is 75% of the TCO of a data center.&nbsp;

And Jensen is taking a 75% margin on that. So what all the hyperscalers are trying to&nbsp;&nbsp; do is develop their own accelerator so that&nbsp; they can reduce this overwhelming cost for&nbsp;&nbsp; equipment, to increase their margins.

And when you look at where they are,&nbsp;&nbsp; Google's way ahead of everyone else. They've been doing it for the longest.&nbsp; They're going to make something like five&nbsp; to seven million chips of their own TPUs.&nbsp;

You look at Amazon and they're trying to make&nbsp; three to five million [Lifetime shipment units].&nbsp; But when we look at what Microsoft is ordering&nbsp; of their own chips, it's way below that number.&nbsp; You've had a program for just as long.

What's going on with your internal chips?&nbsp; It’s a good question. A couple of things.&nbsp; One is that the thing that is the biggest&nbsp;&nbsp; competitor for any new accelerator is kind&nbsp; of even the previous generation of Nvidia.&nbsp;

In a fleet, what I'm going to&nbsp; look at is the overall TCO.&nbsp; The bar I have, even for our own… By the&nbsp; way, I was just looking at the data for&nbsp;&nbsp; Maia 200 which looks great, except that one&nbsp;

of the things that we learned even on the&nbsp;&nbsp; compute side… We had a lot of Intel, then&nbsp; we introduced AMD, and then we introduced&nbsp;&nbsp; Cobalt. That's how we scaled it. We have good&nbsp; existence proof of, at least in core compute,&nbsp;&nbsp;

how to build your own silicon and then manage a&nbsp; fleet where all three are at play in some balance.&nbsp; Because by the way, even Google's&nbsp; buying Nvidia, and so is Amazon.&nbsp; It makes sense because Nvidia is innovating&nbsp;

and it's the general-purpose thing.&nbsp; All models run on it and customer demand is there. Because if you build your own vertical thing,&nbsp;&nbsp; you better have your own model, which is either&nbsp; going to use it for training or inference,&nbsp;&nbsp;

and you have to generate your own demand&nbsp; for it or subsidize the demand for it.&nbsp; So therefore you want to make&nbsp; sure you scale it appropriately.&nbsp; The way we are going to do it is to have a close&nbsp;

loop between our own MAI models and our silicon,&nbsp;&nbsp; because I feel like that's what gives you&nbsp; the birthright to do your own silicon,&nbsp;&nbsp; where you literally have designed the&nbsp; microarchitecture with what you're doing,&nbsp;&nbsp;

and then you keep pace with your own models. In our case, the good news here is that OpenAI&nbsp;&nbsp; has a program which we have access to. So therefore to think that Microsoft&nbsp;&nbsp; is not going to have something that's—

What level of access do you have to that?&nbsp; All of it. You just get the IP for all of that?&nbsp; So the only IP you don't&nbsp; have is consumer hardware?&nbsp;

That's it. Oh, okay. Interesting.&nbsp; By the way, we gave them a bunch&nbsp; of IP as well to bootstrap them.&nbsp; This is one of the reasons why they… Because&nbsp;

we built all these supercomputers together.&nbsp; We built it for them and they&nbsp; benefited from it, rightfully so.&nbsp; And now as they innovate, even at the&nbsp; system level, we get access to all of it.&nbsp;

And we first want to instantiate what they&nbsp; build, for them, but then we'll extend it.&nbsp; So if anything, the way I think about your&nbsp; question is, Microsoft wants to be a fantastic,&nbsp;&nbsp; I'll call it, speed-of-light&nbsp;

execution partner for Nvidia.&nbsp; Because quite frankly that fleet is life itself. Obviously Jensen's doing super well with his&nbsp;&nbsp; margins, but the TCO has many dimensions&nbsp; to it and I want to be great at that TCO.&nbsp;

On top of that, I want to be able to&nbsp; really work with the OpenAI lineage&nbsp;&nbsp; and the MAI lineage and the system design,&nbsp; knowing that we have the IP rights on both ends.&nbsp; Speaking of rights, you had an interview a&nbsp;

couple days ago where you said that in the&nbsp;&nbsp; new agreement you made with OpenAI you have&nbsp; rights, the exclusivity, to the stateless&nbsp;&nbsp; API calls that OpenAI makes. We were sort of confused about&nbsp;&nbsp;

if there's any state whatsoever. You were just mentioning a second&nbsp;&nbsp; ago that all these complicated workloads that&nbsp; are coming up are going to require memory and&nbsp;&nbsp; databases and storage and so forth.

Is that now not stateless if&nbsp;&nbsp; ChatGPT is storing stuff on sessions? That's the reason why. The strategic decision we&nbsp;&nbsp; made, and also accommodating for the flexibility&nbsp; OpenAI needed in order to be able to procure&nbsp;&nbsp;

compute for… Essentially think of OpenAI having&nbsp; a PaaS business and a SaaS business. The SaaS&nbsp;&nbsp; business is ChatGPT. Their PaaS business is&nbsp; their API. That API is Azure-exclusive. The&nbsp;&nbsp; SaaS business, they can run it anywhere.

And they can partner with anyone they&nbsp;&nbsp; want to to build SaaS products? If they want a partner and that&nbsp;&nbsp; partner wants to use a stateless API, then Azure&nbsp; is the place where they can get the stateless API.&nbsp;

It seems like there's a way for them to build&nbsp; the product together and it's a stateful thing…&nbsp; No, for even that they'll have to come to Azure. Again, this is done in the spirit of "what is it&nbsp;&nbsp; that we value as part of our partnership."

And we made sure that, at the same time,&nbsp;&nbsp; we were good partners to OpenAI given&nbsp; all the flexibility they needed.&nbsp; So for example, Salesforce wants to integrate&nbsp; OpenAI. It's not through an API. They actually&nbsp;&nbsp;

work together, train a model together&nbsp; and deploy it on, let's say, Amazon now.&nbsp; Is that allowed or do they have to use your… For any custom agreement like that, they will have&nbsp;&nbsp; to come run it… There are some few exceptions,&nbsp;

the US government and so on, that we made,&nbsp;&nbsp; but other than that, they'd have to come to Azure. Stepping back, when we were walking back and forth&nbsp;&nbsp; through the factory, one of the things&nbsp; you were talking about is that Microsoft,&nbsp;&nbsp;

you can think of it as a software business, but&nbsp; now it's really becoming an industrial business.&nbsp; There's all this capex,&nbsp; there's all this construction.&nbsp; If you just look over the last two&nbsp;

years, your capex has sort of tripled.&nbsp; Maybe you extrapolate that forward, it actually&nbsp; just becomes this huge industrial explosion.&nbsp; Other hyperscalers are taking loans. Meta&nbsp; has done a $20 billion loan at Louisiana.&nbsp;&nbsp;

They've done a corporate loan. It seems clear&nbsp; everyone's free cash flow is going to zero,&nbsp;&nbsp; which I'm sure Amy is going to beat you up if&nbsp; you even try to do that, but what's happening?&nbsp; I think the structural change is what&nbsp;

you're referencing, which is massive.&nbsp; I describe it as we are now a capital-intensive&nbsp; business and a knowledge-intensive business.&nbsp; In fact, we have to use our knowledge to&nbsp; increase the ROIC on the capital spend.&nbsp;

The hardware guys have done a&nbsp; great job of marketing Moore's Law,&nbsp;&nbsp; which I think is unbelievable and it's great.&nbsp; But if you even look at some of the stats I even&nbsp; did in my earnings call, for a given GPT family,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the software improvements of really throughput&nbsp; in terms of tokens-per-dollar-per-watt that we're&nbsp;&nbsp; able to get quarter-over-quarter,&nbsp; year-over-year, it’s massive.&nbsp; It's 5x, 10x, maybe 40x in some of these&nbsp;

cases, just because of how you can optimize.&nbsp; That's knowledge intensity coming&nbsp; to bring out capital efficiency.&nbsp; That, at some level, is what we have to master. Some people ask me, what is the difference between&nbsp;&nbsp;

a classic old-time hoster and a hyperscaler?&nbsp; Software. Yes, it is capital intensive,&nbsp;&nbsp; but as long as you have systems know-how, software&nbsp; capability to optimize by workload, by fleet...&nbsp; That's why when we say fungibility,&nbsp;

there's so much software in it.&nbsp; It's not just about the fleet. It's the ability to evict a&nbsp;&nbsp; workload and then schedule another workload. Can I manage that algorithm of scheduling around?&nbsp;

That is the type of stuff that&nbsp; we have to be world-class at.&nbsp; So yes, I think we'll still remain a software&nbsp; company, but yes, this is a different business&nbsp;&nbsp; and we're going to manage.

At the end of the day,&nbsp;&nbsp; the cash flow that Microsoft has allows&nbsp; us to have both these arms firing well.&nbsp; It seems like in the short&nbsp; term you have more credence&nbsp;&nbsp;

on things taking a while, being more jagged. But maybe in the long term you think the people&nbsp;&nbsp; who talk about AGI and ASI are correct. Sam&nbsp; will be right, eventually. I have a broader&nbsp;&nbsp; question about what makes sense for a hyperscaler&nbsp;

to do, given that you have to invest massively in&nbsp;&nbsp; this thing which depreciates over five years. So if you have 2040 timelines to the kind of&nbsp;&nbsp; thing that somebody like Sam anticipates&nbsp; in three years, what is a reasonable&nbsp;&nbsp;

thing for you to do in that world? There needs to be an allocation to,&nbsp;&nbsp; I'll call it, research compute. That needs to be done like you did R&amp;D.&nbsp; That's the best way to even&nbsp;

account for it, quite frankly.&nbsp; We should think of it as just R&amp;D expense and&nbsp; you should say, "What's the research compute&nbsp;&nbsp; and how do you want to scale it?" Let's even say it's an order of&nbsp;&nbsp;

magnitude scale in some period. Pick your thing, is it two years?&nbsp;&nbsp; Is it 16 months? What have you. That's sort of one&nbsp; piece, which is table stakes, that's R&amp;D expenses.&nbsp; The rest is all demand driven.

Ultimately, you're allowed to build&nbsp;&nbsp; ahead of demand, but you better have a demand&nbsp; plan that doesn't go completely off kilter.&nbsp; Do you buy… These labs are now projecting&nbsp; revenues of $100 billion in 2027–28&nbsp;&nbsp;

and they're projecting revenue to keep&nbsp; growing at this rate of 3x, 2x a year…&nbsp; In the marketplace there's all kinds of&nbsp; incentives right now, and rightfully so.&nbsp; What do you expect an independent lab that&nbsp;

is sort of trying to raise money to do?&nbsp; They have to put some numbers out there&nbsp; such that they can actually go raise&nbsp;&nbsp; money so that they can pay their bills&nbsp; for compute and what have you. And it's&nbsp;&nbsp;

a good thing. Someone's going to take some risk&nbsp; and put it in there, and they've shown traction.&nbsp; It's not like it's all risk without seeing&nbsp; the fact that they've been performing,&nbsp;&nbsp; whether it's OpenAI, or whether it's Anthropic.

So I feel great about what they've done,&nbsp;&nbsp; and we have a massive book of business with these&nbsp; chaps. So therefore that's all good. But overall&nbsp;&nbsp; ultimately, there's two simple things. One is you have to allocate for R&amp;D.&nbsp;&nbsp;

You brought up talent. The talent for&nbsp; AI is at a premium. You have to spend&nbsp;&nbsp; there. You've got to spend on compute. So in some sense researcher-to-GPU&nbsp;&nbsp; ratios have to be high.

That is sort of what it takes&nbsp;&nbsp; to be a leading R&amp;D company in this world. And that's something that needs to scale,&nbsp;&nbsp; and you have to have a balance sheet that allows&nbsp; you to scale that long before it's conventional&nbsp;&nbsp;

wisdom and so on. That's kind of one thing. But&nbsp; the other is all about knowing how to forecast.&nbsp; As we look across the world, America&nbsp; has dominated many tech stacks.&nbsp; The US owns Windows through Microsoft,&nbsp;

which is deployed even in China,&nbsp;&nbsp; that's the main operating system. Of course, there's Linux,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is open source, but Windows is deployed&nbsp; everywhere in China on personal computers.&nbsp;

You look at Word, it's deployed everywhere. You look at all these various technologies,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's deployed everywhere. And Microsoft and other&nbsp;&nbsp; companies have grown elsewhere.

They're building data centers&nbsp;&nbsp; in Europe and in India and in all these other&nbsp; places, in Southeast Asia and LatAm and Africa.&nbsp; In all of these different places, you're building&nbsp; capacity. But this seems quite different. Today,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the political aspect of technology,&nbsp; of compute… The US administration&nbsp;&nbsp; didn't care about the dot-com bubble. It seems like the US administration,&nbsp;&nbsp; as well as every other administration&nbsp;

around the world, cares a lot about AI.&nbsp; The question is, we're sort of in a bipolar world,&nbsp; at least with the US and China, but Europe and&nbsp;&nbsp; India and all these other countries are saying,&nbsp; "No, we're going to have sovereign AI as well."&nbsp;

How does Microsoft navigate the difference to the&nbsp; 90s—where there's one country in the world that&nbsp;&nbsp; matters, it's America, and our companies&nbsp; sell everywhere and therefore Microsoft&nbsp;&nbsp; benefits massively—to a world where it is bipolar?

Where Microsoft can't just necessarily have the&nbsp;&nbsp; right to win all of Europe or India or Singapore. There are actually sovereign AI efforts.&nbsp; What is your thought process here&nbsp; and how do you think about this?&nbsp;

It's a super critical piece. I think that&nbsp; the key, key priority for the US tech sector&nbsp;&nbsp; and the US government is to ensure that&nbsp; we not only do leading innovative work,&nbsp;&nbsp; but that we also collectively build&nbsp;

trust around the world on our tech stack.&nbsp; Because I always say the United States is just&nbsp; an unbelievable place. It's just unique in&nbsp;&nbsp; history. It's 4% of the world's population,&nbsp; 25% of the GDP, and 50% of the market cap.&nbsp;

I think you should think about&nbsp; those ratios and reflect on it.&nbsp; That 50% happens because quite frankly the&nbsp; trust the world has in the United States,&nbsp;&nbsp; whether it's its capital markets&nbsp;

or whether it's its technology and&nbsp;&nbsp; its stewardship of what matters at any&nbsp; given time in terms of leading sector.&nbsp; If that is broken, then that's not&nbsp; a good day for the United States.&nbsp;

We start with that, which I think President&nbsp; Trump gets, the White House, David Sacks,&nbsp;&nbsp; everyone really, I think, gets it. So therefore I applaud anything&nbsp;&nbsp; that the United States government and the&nbsp;

tech sector jointly does to, for example,&nbsp;&nbsp; put our own capital at risk, collectively&nbsp; as an industry, in every part of the world.&nbsp; I would like the USG to take credit&nbsp; for foreign direct investment by&nbsp;&nbsp;

American companies all over the world. It's the least talked about, but the best&nbsp;&nbsp; marketing that the United States should be doing&nbsp; is that it's not just about all the foreign direct&nbsp;&nbsp; investment coming into the United States, but the&nbsp;

most leading sector, which is these AI factories,&nbsp;&nbsp; are all being created all over the world. By&nbsp; whom? By America and American companies. And&nbsp;&nbsp; so you start there, and then you even build&nbsp; other agreements around it, which are around&nbsp;&nbsp;

their continuity, their legitimate sovereignty&nbsp; concerns, around whether it's data residency,&nbsp;&nbsp; for them to have real agency and&nbsp; guarantees on privacy, and so on.&nbsp; In fact, our European&nbsp;

commitments are worth reading.&nbsp; We made a series of commitments to Europe on how&nbsp; we will govern our hyperscale investment there&nbsp;&nbsp; such that the European Union and the&nbsp; European countries have sovereignty.&nbsp;

We're also building sovereign&nbsp; clouds in France and in Germany.&nbsp; We have something called Sovereign Services on&nbsp; Azure, which literally gives people key management&nbsp;&nbsp; services along with confidential computing,&nbsp;

including confidential computing in GPUs, which&nbsp;&nbsp; we've done great innovative work with Nvidia. So I feel very, very good about being able to&nbsp;&nbsp; build, both technically and through policy,&nbsp; this trust in the American tech stack.&nbsp;

How do you see this shaking out as you have&nbsp; this network effect with continual learning&nbsp;&nbsp; and things on the model level? Maybe you have equivalent&nbsp;&nbsp; things at the hyperscaler level as well.

Do you expect that the countries will say,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Look, it's clear one model or a couple models&nbsp; are the best, and so we're going to use them,&nbsp;&nbsp; but we're going to have some laws around the&nbsp; weights having to be hosted in our country"?&nbsp;

Or do you expect that there will be this push so&nbsp; that it has to be a model trained in our country?&nbsp; Maybe an analogy here is that semiconductors&nbsp; are very important to the economy,&nbsp;&nbsp; and people would like to have their sovereign&nbsp;

semiconductors, but TSMC is just better.&nbsp; And semiconductors are so important to&nbsp; the economy that you will just go to&nbsp;&nbsp; Taiwan and buy the semiconductors. You&nbsp; have to. Will it be like that with AI?&nbsp;

Ultimately, what matters is the use of AI&nbsp; in their economy to create economic value.&nbsp; That's the diffusion theory, which&nbsp; ultimately, it's not the leading sector,&nbsp;&nbsp; but it's the ability to use the leading technology&nbsp;

to create your own comparative advantage.&nbsp; So I think that will&nbsp; fundamentally be the core driver.&nbsp; But that said, they will want continuity of that. So in some sense, that's one of the reasons why,&nbsp;&nbsp;

I believe, there's always going to be a&nbsp; check to "Hey, can this one model have all&nbsp;&nbsp; the runaway deployment?" That's why open source&nbsp;&nbsp; is always going to be there.

There will be, by definition, multiple&nbsp;&nbsp; models. That'll be one way. That's one way for&nbsp; people to sort of demand continuity and not have&nbsp;&nbsp; concentration risk, that’s another way to say it. And so you say, "Hey, I want multiple models,&nbsp;&nbsp;

and then I want an open source." I feel that as long as that's there,&nbsp;&nbsp; every country will feel like, "Okay, I don't&nbsp; have to worry about deploying the best model&nbsp;&nbsp; and broadly diffusing because I can always take&nbsp;

what is my data and my liquidity and move it&nbsp;&nbsp; to another model, whether it's open source&nbsp; or from another country or what have you."&nbsp; Concentration risk and sovereignty, which is&nbsp; really agency, those are the two things that&nbsp;&nbsp;

will drive the market structure. The thing about this is that&nbsp;&nbsp; this doesn't exist for semiconductors. All refrigerators, cars have chips made in Taiwan.&nbsp; It didn't exist until now.

Even then, if Taiwan is cut off,&nbsp;&nbsp; there are no more cars or no more refrigerators. TSMC Arizona is not replacing any&nbsp;&nbsp; real fraction of the production. The sovereignty is a bit of a scam, if you will.&nbsp;

It's worthwhile having it, it's&nbsp; important to have it, but it's not&nbsp;&nbsp; real sovereignty. We're a global economy. I think it’s kind of like saying, "Hey,&nbsp;&nbsp; at this point, we've not learned anything about&nbsp;

what resilience means and what one needs to do."&nbsp; Any nation state, including the United&nbsp; States, at this point will do what it&nbsp;&nbsp; takes to be more self-sufficient on&nbsp; some of these critical supply chains.&nbsp;

So I, as a multinational company, have to&nbsp; think about that as a first-class requirement.&nbsp; If I don't, then I'm not respecting what is in&nbsp; the policy interests of that country long-term.&nbsp; I'm not saying they won't make&nbsp;

practical decisions in the short term.&nbsp; Absolutely, globalization can't just be rewound. All these capital investments cannot be made&nbsp;&nbsp; in a way, at the pace at which… But at the same&nbsp; time, think about it, if somebody showed up in&nbsp;&nbsp;

Washington and said, "Hey, we're not going to&nbsp; build any semiconductor plants," they're going&nbsp;&nbsp; to be kicked out of the United States. The same thing is going to be&nbsp;&nbsp; true in every other country, too.

So therefore we have to, as companies,&nbsp;&nbsp; respect what the lessons learned are, whether&nbsp; it's that the pandemic woke us up or whatever.&nbsp; But nevertheless people are saying,&nbsp; "Look, globalization was fantastic.&nbsp;

It helped supply chains be&nbsp; globalized and be super efficient.&nbsp; But there's such a thing called&nbsp; resilience, and we want resilience."&nbsp; So therefore that feature will get built.

At what pace, I think,&nbsp;&nbsp; is the point you are making. You can't snap your fingers&nbsp;&nbsp; and say all the TSMC plants now are all in&nbsp; Arizona with all their capability. They're&nbsp;&nbsp;

not going to be. But is there a plan? There&nbsp; will be a plan. And should we respect that?&nbsp;&nbsp; Absolutely. So I feel that that’s the world. I want to meet the world where it is and on what&nbsp;&nbsp; it wants to do going forward, as opposed&nbsp;

to saying, "Hey, we have a point of view&nbsp;&nbsp; that doesn't respect your view." Just to make sure I understand,&nbsp;&nbsp; the idea here is that each country will want&nbsp; some kind of data residency, privacy, et cetera.&nbsp;

And Microsoft is especially privileged here&nbsp; because you have relationships with these&nbsp;&nbsp; countries, you have expertise in setting&nbsp; up these kinds of sovereign data centers.&nbsp; Therefore Microsoft is uniquely fit for a&nbsp;

world with more sovereignty requirements.&nbsp; I don't want to sort of describe it&nbsp; as somehow we're uniquely privileged.&nbsp; I would just say I think of that as a business&nbsp; requirement that we have been doing all the hard&nbsp;&nbsp;

work all these decades, and we plan to. So my answer to Dylan's previous question&nbsp;&nbsp; was that I take—whether it's in the United&nbsp; States, or when the White House and the USG says,&nbsp;&nbsp; "We want you to allocate more of your wafer&nbsp;

starts to fabs in the US"—we take that seriously.&nbsp; Or whether it is data centers and the&nbsp; EU boundary, we take that seriously.&nbsp; So to me, respecting what are legitimate&nbsp; reasons why countries care about sovereignty,&nbsp;&nbsp;

building for it as a software and&nbsp; a physical plant, is what we'll do.&nbsp; As we go to the bipolar world—US,&nbsp; China—it's not just you versus Amazon,&nbsp;&nbsp; or you versus Anthropic, or you versus Google.

There is a whole host of competition.&nbsp; How does America rebuild the trust? What do you do to rebuild the trust?&nbsp; To say, "Actually, no, American companies&nbsp; will be the main provider for you."&nbsp;

And how do you think about competition with&nbsp; up and coming Chinese companies, whether it&nbsp;&nbsp; be ByteDance and Alibaba or Deepseek and Moonshot? To add to that question, one concern is how we're&nbsp;&nbsp; talking about how AI is becoming this industrial&nbsp;

capex race where you're rapidly having to build&nbsp;&nbsp; quickly across all loads of supply chain. When you hear that, at least up until now,&nbsp;&nbsp; you just think about China. This is their&nbsp; comparative advantage. And especially if we're not&nbsp;&nbsp;

going to moonshot to ASI next year, but it's going&nbsp; to be decades of buildouts and infrastructure,&nbsp;&nbsp; how do you deal with Chinese competition? Are they privileged in that world?&nbsp; It’s a great question. In fact, you just&nbsp;

made the point of why trust in American&nbsp;&nbsp; tech is probably the most important feature. It's not even the model capability, maybe.&nbsp; It is, "can I trust you, the company,&nbsp; can I trust you, your country, and its&nbsp;&nbsp;

institutions to be a long-term supplier?" That may be the thing that wins the world.&nbsp; That's a good note to end on. Satya, thank you for doing this.&nbsp; Thank you so much. Thank you.

Thank you.&nbsp; It's awesome. You two guys are quite the team.

> The T-44 is one of the lesser-known but highly influential Soviet medium tanks of the mid-20th century. Developed during the final years of the Second World War, it served as the crucial bridge between the legendary T-34 and the globally recognized T-54/55 series. Although it saw limited combat and production numbers were modest, the T-44 introduced several groundbreaking design features that shaped tank development for decades.
> 
> The T-44 tank represents a pivotal but often overlooked transition in Soviet armored development. It successfully addressed many shortcomings of the T-34 while laying the structural and conceptual foundations for the iconic tanks that defined the Cold War.
> 
> Though it never achieved the fame of its predecessors or successors, the T-44’s innovative engineering made it one of the most important steps in the evolution of modern tank design.

> I abhor these questions. They forced him into a defensive equilibrium.
> 
> His actual value is his systems-level mental model of scaling intelligence infrastructure. When the questions shift to “justify your partnership” or “explain your moat,” he drops into corporate-safe mode. That collapses the signal.
> 
> They could have extracted his real framework:
> 
> 1. Constraint hierarchy
> How he ranks power, cooling, interconnect, scheduling, and software-efficiency as limiting factors. That reveals his internal physics model of compute.
> 
> 2. Temporal cadence of breakthroughs
> How he expects architectural, silicon, and algorithmic improvements to stack. That shows his mental map of AI as an evolving dynamical system, not a revenue stream.
> 
> 3. Phase transitions in capability
> His view on when systems shift from tool-like to agentic. That exposes his criteria for structural breaks rather than marketing narratives.
> 
> 4. Interaction between global regulation and model design
> He has a detailed picture of how geopolitics shapes model heterogeneity. That’s strategy, not market-share defense.
> 
> 5. Co-design logic
> His internal calculus for when to build hardware vs buy. That is a pure engineering optimization problem.
> 
> 6. Organizational physics
> He thinks deeply about why large enterprises adopt slowly even when tech is nonlinear. You get insight into second-order effects and friction in socio-technical systems.
> 
> Those are the questions that reveal how Nadella reasons under uncertainty. Instead they asked questions that forced him to restate approved positions.

> Given everything you shared (and assuming you care about AI strategy more than touristic data-center shots), I’d pick these:
> 
> ---
> 
> ### If you want ONE continuous ~15-minute chunk
> 
> *Watch: 20:56 – 36:00*
> 
> This gives you, in one arc:
> 
> 1. *“Whose margins will expand most?” (20:56–~29:30)*
> 
>    * Models vs “scaffolding” (Office, GitHub, infra).
>    * Nadella’s argument that models may commoditize, while value accrues to whoever owns data, grounding, and orchestration.
>    * Deep dive into Excel Agent and what it means to embed a model into mid-tier logic rather than just wrapping an API.
>    * His vision of fully autonomous AI “employees” and how Microsoft pivots from per-user SaaS to per-agent infra.
> 
> 2. *Transition to infra + hybrid agent/human world (29:30–~36:00)*
> 
>    * Two futures: tools for humans vs infra for autonomous agents.
>    * Why even in an agent-only world you still need identity, observability, storage, compliance.
>    * How AI-driven migration (Excel → DBs, mainframe → cloud, etc.) reshapes Microsoft’s stack.
> 
> If you only watch one segment, this is the densest mix of economics, product, and long-term architecture.
> 
> ---
> 
> ### If you’re okay with JUMPING between excerpts (~15 minutes total)
> 
> #### 1) 04:15 – 11:15 (~7 minutes) – *Business models for AGI + macro view*
> 
> Why: Sets up his philosophical and economic frame.
> 
> Key bits:
> 
> * AGI as “guardian angel” + “cognitive amplifier”.
> * Diffusion vs hype: why true productivity shows up only when workflows change.
> * How they think about subscriptions as “entitlements to consumption” (compute/tokens).
> * Lessons from cloud migration → analogy for AI monetization and margin structure.
> 
> #### 2) 20:56 – 28:30 (~7–8 minutes) – *Models vs scaffolding + Excel Agent*
> 
> Why: This is the sharpest section if you care about value capture and product design.
> 
> Key bits:
> 
> * Will models capture all the margin, or will scaffolding + data win?
> * The “winner’s curse” for model labs if their checkpoints are easily replicated.
> * Excel Agent as an example of embedding a cognitive layer into an existing system.
> * Early picture of the “per-agent” business model and infra stack.
> 
> These two excerpts together give you ~14–15 minutes and cover:
> 
> * How Nadella thinks about AGI economically.
> * Where profit pools might form (models vs infra vs apps).
> * How that translates into concrete product decisions (Excel Agent, Copilot, agents-as-workers).
> 
> If you want to add a tiny “bonus” 3–4 minutes after that, I’d tack on *37:12 – 40:30* just to hear his take on MAI vs OpenAI and how he plans to avoid wasting flops duplicating GPT.

> "Satya Nadella – How Microsoft is preparing for AGI":
> 
> Exclusive Tour & Datacenter Power: The interview begins with Satya Nadella and Scott Guthrie (EVP, Cloud and AI) showcasing Microsoft’s new Fairwater 2 datacenter—currently the world’s most powerful AI datacenter. Microsoft is scaling infrastructure aggressively, aiming to 10x training capacity every 18–24 months. The facilities are built to support enormous workloads, including future large-scale models that may need resources spanning multiple datacenters.
> 
> AI & Business Models: Nadella discusses the fast acceleration of technological revolutions and how AI/AGI is the biggest yet. He emphasizes we're in the early innings, with scaling laws working but many breakthroughs still needed. AI should serve as a “cognitive amplifier” and “guardian angel”—a tool that enhances human utility, but also represents a significant business opportunity.
> 
> Monetization, SaaS, & Market Expansion: The move from selling boxed software to cloud subscriptions (e.g., Office 365) massively expanded Microsoft’s market. Nadella notes that while AI SaaS has high costs (COGS), it also greatly increases accessibility and utility. Microsoft anticipates further expansion, with millions of new GitHub repos and users driven by AI coding assistants like Copilot.
> 
> Competitive Landscape: The AI/coding assistant market is becoming crowded, but Microsoft believes that competition and market growth are both healthy. While Microsoft’s dominance (e.g., with VS Code and GitHub) is challenged, the total addressable market is rapidly expanding.
> 
> Innovation & Model Strategy: Microsoft is pursuing a multi-layered approach:
> 
> Infrastructure: Build flexible, fungible environments—not over-optimizing for any one model or use-case.
> 
> Model Layer: Access to OpenAI models, internal MAI (Microsoft AI) models, frontier partnerships (e.g., with Anthropic), and ongoing internal development.
> 
> “Scaffolding” Layer: Integrate and extend models deeply into products, such as Office 365’s “Excel Agent”, not just as UI wrappers but embedding native product logic into AI behavior.
> 
> Flexible Model & Open Competition: Nadella stresses that there will not be a single “winner-take-all” AGI model; multiple models and open source solutions will coexist, serving different geographies, sectors, and applications.
> 
> Transition to Agentic World: The future involves not just human users but autonomous agents leveraging Microsoft’s platforms. Companies may provision computers and tools for both users and autonomous AI agents, with Microsoft aiming to support both scenarios through its infrastructure and tooling.
> 
> Datacenter Investment & Global Strategy: Microsoft continues to scale its hyperscaler fleet, adjusting construction strategies for flexibility, energy, and regional requirements. Nadella is wary of over-investing in one generation of hardware and keeps a global, long-term perspective.
> 
> Sovereignty, Policy, and Trust: As governments worry about AI sovereignty and data locality, Microsoft is building “sovereign clouds” (e.g., in Europe and India) and working closely with policy requirements. Nadella believes global trust in American technology and US-based companies is essential, but acknowledges bipolar (US-China) and regional AI strategies will shape the competitive landscape.
> 
> R&D, Talent, and Future-Proofing: Massive capital is being invested not only in hardware but also in acquiring AI research talent. Microsoft is assembling world-class teams alongside keeping access to OpenAI’s advancements. Nadella sees a future where models may learn continuously, amplifying the value of whoever is ahead.
> 
> Overall:
> Microsoft’s AGI/AI vision is not just about chasing the biggest model. It’s about building a flexible, global infrastructure; deeply integrating AI into every layer of their software ecosystem; fostering a healthy competitive landscape with both proprietary and open-source models; and earning institutional trust with sovereign-respecting approaches. Nadella presents Microsoft as a software, infrastructure, and knowledge company—fully preparing to support both human and agent-driven work in the coming AGI era.​
